data.title: Asian trading is mixed as worries about AI-related issues grow
data.description:
TOKYO (AP) — Asians shares were trading mixed early Friday, as worries about the future of artificial intelligence grew after Alphabet’s stock drop dragged on U.S. markets.

Japan’s benchmark Nikkei 225 dropped 2.6% to 62,960.60. The Bank of Japan is closing a two-day monetary policy board meeting, but most analysts expect no action this time around after the central bank raised its benchmark rate to 1.25% last month.

The U.S. has also been pressuring Japan to raise rates because of concerns about the weakening yen. In currency trading, the U.S. dollar fell to 157.50 Japanese yen from 157.65 yen. The euro cost $1.1197, up from $1.1181.

Australia’s S&P/ASX 200 rose 0.5% to 8,937.60. South Korea’s Kospi declined 5.4% to 5,618.76, as shares in SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics both slipped in morning trading.

Shares related to the great market interest in AI have tended to be volatile, because some issues, including chip makers, get pushed up because of that interest, but then may decline because of worries about supplies, for instance.

Hong Kong’s Hang Seng added 1.2% to 23,225.69, while the Shanghai Composite lost 0.9% to 3,618.14.

On Wall Street, the S&P 500 fell 0.3% for its first loss in four days, even though the wide majority of stocks rose within the index and across Wall Street. The Nasdaq composite tumbled 1.4%, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 132 points, or 0.3%.

Alphabet is one of the most influential stocks on Wall Street because it’s one of the largest, and the Class A shares of its stock fell 12.6% for their worst day since they began trading more than 20 years ago.

All told, the S&P 500 fell 23.59 points to 7,720.39 Thursday. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 132.54 to 52,342.56, and the Nasdaq composite tumbled 365.13 to 26,184.72.

In the bond market, the yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.94% from 5.05% late Wednesday. It’s been generally pulling back since it topped 5.30% earlier this month and touched its highest level since 2002.

In energy trading, benchmark U.S. crude gained 2.80% to $104.86 a barrel. Brent crude, the international standard, edged up 2.54% to $117.80 a barrel.

“This week is less about broad conviction and more about proof. Big Tech now has to show that the spending binge still deserves the market’s faith,” Stephen Innes of SPI Asset Management said in a commentary.

Industrial companies had some of the biggest losses. Caterpillar fell 2.4%.

Treasury yields in the U.S. edged higher following sharp drops on Thursday.

Yields have been rising globally, partly over worries about governments taking on too much debt. Inflation also remains a concern and is stubbornly well above 3% in the U.S. That prompted the Federal Reserve to raise its benchmark interest rate at its last meeting in an effort to cool inflation.

Wall Street expects the central bank to hold rates steady at its meeting this week, but is leaning heavily toward another rate hike in December.

AI-related stocks have been swinging on worries that their boom may be under threat because of how expensive it’s become to borrow money to build data centers and buy more AI chips. Investors fear their prices shot too high during a yearslong frenzy, even though companies in the industry continue to report growth.

Meta Platforms, which is pushing its Muse AI agent, lost 7% after reporting stronger revenue for the latest quarter than analysts expected, though its profit fell short. Tesla fell 3.1% after reporting a stronger profit for the summer than analysts expected, though its revenue was weaker than forecast.

The global tide against AI stocks knocked Nvidia down 4.4%. Because the chip giant is the largest company on Wall Street by total value, movements for its stock carry more weight on the S&P 500 than any other, and it was the single strongest force pulling the index lower.

CoreWeave, which has borrowed money to buy Nvidia’s AI chips that it rents out to customers over the cloud, has been particularly shaky in recent weeks because of worries about its debt. It dropped 10.1%.

Worries about big government debt loads and strained budgets are hanging over almost every developed economy. Protests across France have raised pressure on the government to increase spending, which could add further to its debt.

In the United States, such concerns, along with high inflation, signals of a still-strong U.S. economy and other factors, have pushed yields in the U.S. bond market recently to their highest levels in decades.

But U.S. yields fell sharply Thursday in a signal that investors were buying U.S. government bonds in search of something safer to own as AI stocks tumbled.

The yield on the 10-year Treasury tumbled to 4.97% from 5.13% late Wednesday and from more than 5.30% earlier this month. That’s a major move for the bond market.

data.title: Indonesian leader rejects market downgrade warning after stock market sell-off
data.description:
JAKARTA, Indonesia (AP) — Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto rejected a warning from Morgan Stanley Capital International that could lead to the country’s stock market being downgraded, saying his country would not be pressured by external parties.

Prabowo delivered a fiery speech at a gathering of his Cabinet on Wednesday, accusing the New York-based global index provider of attempting to pressure Indonesia after it said last week it was considering downgrading the country’s equity market as a “standalone” market.

“Our country continues to face all sorts of disturbances, including the MSCI. They are trying to intimidate us,” Prabowo told his Cabinet in a speech broadcast on the government’s official YouTube channel.

“I simply want to tell MSCI: the Indonesian nation fears no one and will never back down,” Prabowo said. “We have the strength, the courage and we are willing to make sacrifices, and we refuse to surrender.”

MSCI said on Oct. 15 it opened a consultation on a proposal to downgrade Indonesia’s market status. It said it was weighing ejecting Indonesia from “emerging” status and into the “standalone” status, which could cause multi-billion-dollar capital outflows.

The index provider said its concerns center on coordinated trading practices in Indonesia’s stock market and whether authorities have taken sufficient steps to address them. It said its assessments are based on transparent and rules-based methodologies.

The warning has rattled investors and contributed to a sharp sell-off in Indonesian stocks over the past two trading sessions. A downgrade could reduce Indonesia’s attractiveness to international investors and potentially prompt capital outflows from funds that track emerging market indexes.

“MSCI will continue to monitor developments in the Indonesian market and engage with market participants and authorities,” the company said in a statement.

A government spokesperson, Syahganda Nainggolan, said Thursday that Prabowo’s remarks were not intended as a challenge to MSCI but as an invitation to dialogue, provided it takes place without pressure or coercion.

“The president highly values constructive engagement and dialogue with rating institutions such as MSCI,” Nainggolan said.

Prabowo, a former army special forces commander who took office in 2024, has frequently employed nationalist rhetoric and has often warned of foreign efforts to influence or undermine Indonesia. During Wednesday’s remarks, he again referred to outside interference, although he did not provide details.
